analysis.one_liner: Caps credit card late fees, bounced-check fees, and ATM surcharges, bans forced arbitration clauses, and requires banks to get customer permission before sharing personal data.
analysis.headline: Introduced in April 2000 with three cosponsors, the bill never received a committee hearing or vote and died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have limited the fees banks and credit card companies charge ordinary customers: it would cap credit card late fees and bounced-check fees at roughly the industry's actual cost, ban most out-of-network ATM surcharges, and require banks to give customers three free teller transactions a month. It would also have banned forced arbitration clauses in consumer contracts, required banks to get a customer's permission before sharing or selling that customer's personal financial information, and made it a crime to obtain someone's bank records by pretending to be them. The bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary bank customers and credit card holders would gain. The bill would cap credit card late fees and bounced-check fees at twice the government-measured average cost of handling them, ban fees charged by an ATM owner when a customer uses another bank's machine, require three free in-person teller transactions a month, and require bank regulators to consider "lifeline banking" needs of low-income communities during examinations [S3][S2]. All consumers signing standardized contracts would keep their right to sue, because mandatory arbitration clauses would be treated as an unfair and deceptive trade practice [S3]. Customers of banks, brokers, and insurers would have to affirmatively consent before their nonpublic personal financial information could be shared or sold, would gain the right to see and correct information shared with third parties, and would get fraud hotlines and protection against identity thieves who use false pretenses to obtain their records [S3][S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Bank customers and credit card holders

how_it_helps.text: Caps credit card late fees at twice the Federal Reserve's published estimate of the average cost to creditors of a late payment, or the outstanding balance if smaller
Caps bounced-check fees the same way and bars a receiving bank from charging the depositor for handling a check that bounced or for reversing a provisional settlement
Bans surcharges at an ATM when the transaction runs through a national or regional network and does not involve a customer of the machine's owner

Treats any mandatory binding arbitration clause in a standardized consumer contract as an unenforceable unfair and deceptive trade practice, while allowing consumers to agree to arbitration after a dispute arises

Rewrites the Gramm-Leach-Bliley privacy title to require a customer's affirmative opt-in consent before a financial institution shares nonpublic personal information with affiliates or outside companies, bans denying service to customers who refuse, and gives customers the right to examine and dispute information shared with third parties

Makes it a federal crime, punishable by up to five years in prison, to obtain bank customer information through false pretenses or forged documents, with enhanced penalties for organized schemes over $100,000
Requires creditors and credit bureaus to publish toll-free antifraud hotline numbers on consumer reports and lets consumers place a fraud watch on their file
Requires three free in-person teller transactions per month at insured banks and directs regulators to weigh the lifeline banking needs of low-income communities when examining institutions

analysis.who_pays: Banks and credit card issuers would bear the cost: the bill caps the late fees and bounced-check fees that generate billions in annual revenue, bans the out-of-network ATM surcharges that 77 percent of surveyed Illinois voters wanted banned, requires three free teller transactions a month, and replaces the financial industry's "opt-out" data-sharing regime under the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act with an "opt-in" rule, cutting off a lucrative channel for selling customer information to marketers [S3][S2]. Businesses that write forced arbitration clauses into consumer contracts would lose a tool for keeping disputes out of court [S3].

drawbacks.text: Because the fee caps are set at twice the industry's measured cost rather than at a fixed dollar amount, banks that lose fee revenue could make up the difference through other charges, such as higher minimum balances or account maintenance fees, which would fall hardest on customers who keep small balances
Banning out-of-network ATM surcharges could lead machine owners to withdraw ATMs from low-income and rural locations where transactions are least profitable, reducing convenient access to cash

The arbitration ban defines a consumer as 'any individual' and covers every standardized consumer contract, not just financial products, a breadth that even some consumer-protection supporters might have narrowed

Requiring affirmative opt-in consent and annual compliance with detailed notices would impose significant paperwork and systems costs on banks, credit unions, brokers, and insurers, and the bill lets agencies grant waivers and delayed effective dates, adding uncertainty

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer benefits are concrete and would reach nearly every household: lower late and bounced-check fees, fewer ATM surcharges, the right to sue instead of arbitrate, and control over who buys their financial data. The bill's design is defensible but not perfect: tying fee caps to regulators' annual estimates of industry cost is flexible yet could invite disputes over the numbers, and fee caps can be evaded through new charges. The largest honest cost falls on financial firms, whose fee and data revenue would shrink; whether some of that cost reappears as other fees on customers is a real risk the bill does not fully address. On balance, the benefits to ordinary consumers outweigh the costs, and the bill's death means consumers continued paying the fees the surveys cited, including late fees above $25 from a majority of surveyed issuers.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in House subcommittees from April 2000 until the Congress ended in January 2001, with no hearing, markup, or vote ever scheduled.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 13, 2000 by Rep. Jan Schakowsky and referred to two committees, Banking and Financial Services and Commerce
On the day of introduction it was sent to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit, and on April 25, 2000 to the Subcommittee on Finance and Hazardous Materials
No further action appears in the record: no hearings, markups, votes, or floor action before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001

The bill's findings cited a survey finding that 67 of 116 credit card issuers charged late fees above $25, and a survey finding that large banks raised bounced-check fees by 10 percent from 1997 to 1999

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks, credit card issuers, and companies that profit from customer data and forced arbitration are better off, because the fee caps, opt-in privacy rule, and arbitration ban never came to pass. Consumers saw no change in late fees, ATM surcharges, or data-sharing practices.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Banks, credit card issuers, and data marketers

for.name: Rep. Jan Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its lead sponsor

against.name: Rep. James Leach
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Banking and Financial Services
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration; after the April 2000 subcommittee referrals, no markup, hearing, or vote appears in the action history for the rest of the Congress

against.name: Banks and credit card issuers
against.what_they_did: Opposed fee caps and opt-in privacy rules; the bill received no committee action despite being filed months before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Democrats and the bill died without a recorded vote in a committee led by Republicans, so no roll-call shows how the parties would have split.

industries.note: Late fees would be capped at twice the Federal Reserve-measured average cost of a missed payment; the bill's own findings cite 67 of 116 issuers charging more than $25 per late fee. Late fees are a major revenue line, so the cap transfers money back to cardholders.

The bill caps bounced-check fees, bans out-of-network ATM surcharges, mandates three free teller transactions a month, and adds lifeline-banking criteria to regulators' examinations. It also replaces the Gramm-Leach-Bliley opt-out regime with opt-in consent, ending the default ability to share and sell customer data to marketers.

Under the rewritten privacy title, banks could not share account numbers for telemarketing or electronic marketing, and nonpublic personal information could not flow to nonaffiliated third parties without affirmative customer consent. Marketers lose access to a large stream of financial data.

Mandatory arbitration clauses in standardized consumer contracts would be unenforceable and treated as an unfair and deceptive trade practice, so disputes would return to the courts. Only agreements signed after a dispute actually arises would still count.
